2.text: to look upon. (She spits, and with the saliva smears her whole body from

3.text: head to foot. Indeed, the husband begins to be drawn towards her.)

4.text: “I, who was till now neglected, I turn myself back towards him; I make

5.text: myself into a deadly pain for him. Let him be attracted by the smell from

6.text: here, and have a desire for me. If I reject him, let him be still more

7.text: insistent!” And really the husband leaves off his former passion.

8.text: Told by Äqaˊñña (woman) in the village of Čeˊčin, 1901.

10.text: The Raven sees carrion lying in the wilderness. “Let me go and call

11.text: the neighbors. I have found game that is lying quite motionless.” A crowd

12.text: of ravens come to the carrion and alight on it. “Stop there! Let the chief

13.text: come here!” The chief comes, — the Raven chief. “I will begin from the

14.text: spot around the eyes.” (He alights, and, turning up his sleeves, takes out

15.text: his knife. The others do the same. Their knives glisten in the sun.

16.text: Nevertheless, they are only raven-beaks.) I spread an enchanted noose.

17.text: One knife is entangled in it. Nevertheless, it is a raven-beak. The Raven

18.text: wants it back. “Give me back my knife!” says he. “How can I live without

19.text: my knife?” But the fact is, that it is only his own beak. “Give me back

20.text: my knife, my only one.” — “I will not.” — “What shall I give to buy it

21.text: off?” — “Give me the power on such and such a man!” Then the Raven,

22.text: in order to regain the knife, will give one of his incantations to be used for

25.text: 14. INCANTATIONS AGAINST THE RIVALS IN A FOOT-RACE.

26.text: (a) I get the line of the Spider-Woman, and make of it my lasso. This

27.text: I throw on the person “doomed to anger.” His whole body becomes wound

28.text: around and around with it, and then he soon tires, loses his strength, and

29.text: wants to sit down. If he does not, he becomes heated quickly, is covered

30.text: with sweat, and blood spurts from his nose. He spits out blood, and can-

31.text: not keep up with his rival.²
31.note: Footnote reference: superscript U+00B2, tight against the period, per §2.10.

32.text: Told by a Reindeer Chukchee of the Kolyma Country.

33.text: (b) If I desire to rob somebody of swiftness in running, I bring the trunk
33.note: Machine draft reads '(6)'; raster clearly shows italic letter '(b)', the enumeration item following (a) at line 26.

34.text: of a tree from across the sea. I keep the trunk in my teeth. The trunk

35.text: has many branches. These I put down across the road of my adversary.

36.text: He will stumble over them, and his speed will be hampered.

37.text: Told by Scratching-Woman (man) at Mariinsky Post, 1900.
